content: The study by Bauserman et al. (2015) evaluated the impact of caterpillar cereal consumption on various health outcomes in children aged 6 to 18 months. The study defined a greater amount of caterpillar cereal as 30 grams daily for children aged 6–12 months and 45 grams daily for children aged 12–18 months. A lesser amount was defined as no caterpillar cereal consumption. Follow-ups were conducted at 6 and 12 months. The results showed no significant differences in height-for-age z-scores (HAZ) or weight-for-height z-scores (WHZ) between groups at any age, with the quality of evidence rated as very low. The study also assessed anemia (hemoglobin ≤10 g/dL) and found that children consuming caterpillar cereal had a significant reduction in anemia compared to those who did not consume it. Hemoglobin concentrations were significantly higher in children consuming greater amounts of caterpillar cereal compared to those consuming none. However, serum ferritin levels were significantly lower in children consuming greater amounts of caterpillar cereal, while transferrin receptor concentrations were similar between groups. The quality of evidence for these outcomes was rated as very low. Another study by Thorsdottir et al. (2003) examined the effects of cow’s milk consumption on hemoglobin, serum ferritin, transferrin receptor levels, and mean corpuscular volume (MCV) in children aged 9–12 months. A greater amount of cow’s milk was defined as >500 grams, while a lesser amount was defined as <500 grams. The study, which was observational, reported no significant differences in hemoglobin, ferritin, transferrin receptor levels, or MCV between groups. The quality of evidence was rated as very low. Krasevec et al. (2017) and Marinda et al. (2018) investigated the variety of animal-source foods (ASF) consumed by children aged 6–23 months. Krasevec et al. categorized ASF consumption into 0, 1, 2, or 3 types, while Marinda et al. compared fish consumption with milk/milk products. Significant differences in stunting were observed in children consuming 3 types of ASF compared to those consuming 0 or 1 type. Similarly, children consuming 2 types of ASF had lower stunting rates compared to those consuming 1 type. However, no significant differences were observed between children consuming 1 type versus 0 types of ASF. The quality of evidence was rated as low. The systematic review aimed to assess the effects of differing frequencies, amounts, and varieties of ASF on dietary and health outcomes in children. A total of 31 studies were included, with 13 focusing on frequency, 18 on amount, and 2 on variety. Most studies were observational, and only two could be meta-analyzed. The review found inconsistent results and low-quality evidence for the impact of ASF on growth outcomes, anemia prevalence, and nutritional status. The heterogeneity of study designs, metrics, and outcomes limited the ability to draw definitive conclusions. The review highlighted significant data gaps and methodological limitations, including the lack of standardized metrics for frequency and variety of ASF consumption, incomplete reporting of key details, and reliance on single studies for many outcomes. The overall quality of evidence was rated as low, and future research is needed to address these gaps and improve the reliability of findings.
